summary: Discusses how a node chooses which lower-priority TE LSPs to preempt when a higher-priority one needs room, and how preempted LSPs are rerouted by their head-end routers. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: If a VIP needs seats on a full bus, someone has to give up theirs. This explains how a router picks which paths to bump so as few people as possible are bothered.

questions: how does mpls handle high priority traffic
how do you tune preemption policies
subtitle: Choosing which network paths to bump when a VIP path needs the space.

tldr.problem: When a high-priority Label Switched Path (LSP) needs to be established but the network is full, a router must decide which lower-priority LSPs to preempt (kick off their paths) to make room.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a flexible heuristic algorithm that weighs four criteria: the priority of paths being preempted, the number of paths being removed, the bandwidth being reclaimed, and the likelihood those paths can find new routes.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can tune the algorithm to match their priorities: minimize disruptions, minimize blocking, maximize efficiency, or balance multiple goals.

today: RFC 4829 is Informational and remains a reference for how MPLS networks implement preemption policies. It provides guidance for tuning traffic engineering in networks that differentiate by priority and require QoS guarantees.

sections.title: What is LSP Preemption
sections.content:
In MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) networks, traffic flows are sent along predetermined paths called Label Switched Paths (LSPs). Each LSP has a priority and a bandwidth reservation on every link it uses.

When a new high-priority LSP arrives and there is not enough available bandwidth on some link in its path, the network must preempt (remove) some existing lower-priority LSPs to make room. The preempted LSPs are then rerouted by their originating routers, trying to find alternate paths through the network.

The challenge: which LSPs should be preempted? Preempting the wrong ones can cause a cascade of further preemptions as rerouted paths collide with other traffic, wasting bandwidth and destabilizing the network.
sections.plainLanguage: When a high-priority phone call comes in but the network has no free space, the router has to kick some lower-priority data off its current path. The question is: which one to pick?

sections.title: Why This Problem Matters
sections.content:
Networks with Differentiated Services (DiffServ) and Traffic Engineering explicitly assign priorities to traffic and preemption as a tool to guarantee that important traffic (voice, video, financial data) gets through. The problem has multiple competing goals:

  • Minimize cascading: If you preempt a high-priority path for the sake of making room, that path might itself preempt others when rerouted, creating a cascade of disruptions.
  • Minimize number of preemptions: Rerouting is expensive and disruptive; fewer preemptions mean fewer LSPs to move.
  • Minimize wasted bandwidth: If a large LSP is preempted when only a small amount of bandwidth is needed, the extra space is wasted.
  • Maximize reroute success: A preempted LSP that cannot find an alternate route is lost entirely, worse than staying on its original path.

Different network operators care about these goals differently. The RFC provides a single flexible algorithm that can be tuned to prioritize any combination of them.
sections.plainLanguage: You want to pick the passenger with the lowest-priority ticket, but also one with a small bag so others can use the freed space, and one whose destination is easy to reach by another route.

sections.title: The Preemption Heuristic Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC defines an algorithm that scores each preemptable LSP using a weighted objective function. For each candidate LSP, the algorithm calculates a cost H that combines four factors:

  • Priority cost (alpha): how bad is it to preempt a higher-priority LSP?
  • Rerouting cost (beta): penalize preempting many small LSPs (expensive to reroute each one).
  • Bandwidth match cost (gamma): prefer preempting LSPs close in size to the bandwidth needed (reduces waste).
  • Large LSP cost (theta): prefer preempting many small LSPs over few large ones (they have better reroute chances).

The algorithm sorts all preemptable LSPs by cost and selects the ones with the lowest cost that free up enough bandwidth. A network operator configures the weight (alpha, beta, gamma, theta) to tune the algorithm. For example, setting alpha=1, beta=10, gamma=0, theta=0 means prioritize minimizing preemptions, then by priority.
sections.plainLanguage: The router calculates a score for each passenger: lower priority = lower score, smaller bags = lower score, traveling to a reachable destination = lower score. Pick the passengers with the lowest scores until you have enough space.

sections.title: How Different Tunings Change the Outcome
sections.content:
The RFC runs detailed examples on a single link with 16 LSPs and a request for 175 Mbps. With different weight settings:

  • Priority only (alpha=1, others=0): 5 very-low-priority LSPs preempted (191 Mbps freed). High disruption but avoids cascading.
  • Minimize number (beta=1, others=0): Only 2 LSPs preempted (185 Mbps freed). Low disruption but preempts higher-priority traffic, risking cascades.
  • Balance priority and number (alpha=1, beta=10): 3 LSPs preempted. Sweet spot between goals.
  • Minimize blocking (theta=1, others=0): 8 small LSPs preempted (181 Mbps freed). More rerouting work but small LSPs are likely to find new paths.

A large simulation on a 150-node network with 18,306 LSPs showed that tuning for blocking probability minimization (HBlock) gave the best overall results: fewest LSPs blocked, lowest cascading, and lowest wasted bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick by priority only: lots of people move, but they are the lowest priority. Pick by number: fewer people move, but might include VIPs. Pick by bag size: moderate results. Pick by who can easily get another flight: some disruption but everyone finds a seat.

sections.title: Distributed vs. Centralized Decisions
sections.content:
The RFC discusses where the preemption decision happens. In a distributed approach, each router along the path independently runs the algorithm on links where congestion occurs. This is simpler and faster but may miss global optimizations.

In a centralized approach, a single point (the path computation engine) decides which LSPs to preempt across the entire path. This is more optimal but requires storing the entire network state and adds setup latency.

The RFC chooses the distributed approach because current Internet protocols (OSPF, IS-IS) are distributed and because dynamic networks change too quickly for centralized decisions to remain accurate. Each node preempts only on its own links, making decisions with local bandwidth information.
sections.plainLanguage: Every bus stop decides independently which passenger to bump when the bus is full (simple, fast, but imperfect). Or one central office decides for all buses (optimal but slow and hard to keep up to date).
